rules.title: createApp owns the only frame loop
rules.rationale: A second loop runs outside the fixed clock, so its work is not part of a tick: it sees torn state, it is invisible to `app.tick()` in a headless test, and it keeps running after `dispose`. In strict mode a module's `ctx.loop` refuses to take subscribers for exactly this reason.

rules.title: Take randomness from ctx.rng and time from frame
rules.rationale: `Math.random`, `Date.now` and `performance.now` make the same seed and the same tick sequence produce different worlds, which turns every replay, snapshot test and bug report into a coin flip. Strict mode traps all three for the duration of a lifecycle hook.

rules.title: Fork the rng per consumer, by label
rules.rationale: Consumers drawing from one stream are coupled by draw order: adding a tree reshuffles every rock placed after it. A fork is derived from a label hash, so each consumer keeps its stream no matter what else exists. The runtime already forks per module id; fork again per feature.
rules.right: const trees = ctx.rng.fork('trees'); const height = trees.range(1, 3)

rules.title: Build into ctx.root, never straight into ctx.scene
rules.rationale: The root is the module's scope: the runtime attaches it at mount, detaches and disposes it at teardown, and can hide or reorder the whole feature by touching one object. Objects added straight to the scene are adopted as a fallback, but they are no longer yours to reason about.

rules.title: Route every GPU allocation through ctx.own
rules.rationale: three.js never frees GPU memory for you. An owned resource is disposed in reverse order at teardown whether the module remembered or not, which is the difference between remounting a scene a hundred times and losing the context on the twelfth.
rules.wrong: const map = new THREE.DataTexture(data, 64, 64)   // never disposed

rules.title: Never write app state from inside a lifecycle hook
rules.rationale: A store write mid-tick means the modules updated before it and the modules updated after it saw different worlds in the same tick — the tick stops being reproducible. `ctx.commit` queues the patch and the runtime drains it at the tick boundary, in module order then emission order.
rules.right: update (state, frame, ctx) { ctx.commit({ speed: state.speed + 1 }) }

rules.title: Only a module that owns a state key may commit
rules.rationale: Unscoped commits from several modules race for the same keys and the last drain wins, silently. `defineScopedModule(at, initial, …)` gives the module one key: it reads that key and its commits merge into that key, so two modules can never collide.
rules.wrong: defineModule({ name: 'hud', update: (s, f, ctx) => ctx.commit({ score: 1 }) })

rules.title: select is a pure, cheap projection
rules.rationale: It runs once per module per tick, before any scene work. Allocating or reading the scene from it makes the read path a write path and puts a garbage-collection pause in the frame budget.

rules.title: Resolve only what you declared in requires/optional
rules.rationale: The runtime orders providers before consumers using the declarations. An undeclared resolve happens to work while the mount order is lucky and breaks the day somebody reorders `use: []`.

rules.title: Publish every capability you declare, during build
rules.rationale: Consumers resolve in `start`, one phase after every build. A declared-but-unpublished capability turns that into an undefined at the far end of the app instead of a mount failure here.
rules.wrong: provides: [ CameraRig ], build () { /* forgot to provide */ }

rules.title: One render hook wins — know which
rules.rationale: The last module in resolved order that defines `render` owns the draw, and a top-level `AppOptions.render` overrides every module. Two composers mounted together is not an error, it is one composer silently never drawing.
rules.right: use: [ postProcessing({ effects }) ]   // one claim, ordered last

rules.title: Generate in build, animate in update
rules.rationale: Allocating in `update` runs at tick rate: it rebuilds buffers the GPU has already uploaded and produces a sawtooth of garbage collection that reads as a frame-rate bug. Strict mode counts objects added to the root during update and reports the growth.

rules.title: Always pass loop.fps explicitly, including 0
rules.rationale: The cap lives on a shared page-global framecapper, so a scene that omits it inherits whatever the last scene on the page asked for — which is how one embedded demo pins a whole site to 30fps.

rules.title: Keep modules/assets DOM-free and SSR-safe
rules.rationale: Textures are `DataTexture`, never a canvas, which is the only reason the asset layer runs in a headless test and inside a server render. One `document.createElement` undoes it for everybody.

rules.title: Mark pooled resources shared before disposing a tree
rules.rationale: `disposeScene` frees everything it walks, pooled materials included. One kit material shared between props, disposed from one owner's teardown, blanks every other prop still using it — which reads as a rendering bug, not a lifecycle one.
rules.wrong: disposeScene(root)   // root holds the shared kit material
rules.right: material.userData.shared = true   // or dispose per module

rules.title: Module names are unique and stable
rules.rationale: The name is the rng fork label and the handle id. Two modules called `props` draw the same random stream and shadow each other in diagnostics; renaming one changes its world.

rules.title: Lifecycle hooks are synchronous
rules.rationale: An async hook resolves after the phase it belongs to has finished: the runtime has already started the next module, or already disposed this one. Load first, then mount the module with what you loaded.
rules.wrong: async build (ctx) { const gltf = await load(url); ctx.root.add(gltf.scene) }
